name: Gorkha
tagline: Hilltop palace where Prithvi Narayan Shah began the making of Nepal
meta_description: Gorkha travel guide: Gorkha Durbar, Kalika temple, Gorakhnath cave, Gorkha Museum, the climb from the bazaar and travel from Kathmandu or Pokhara.
summary: Gorkha is the hill town where the Shah dynasty ruled a small kingdom and from where Prithvi Narayan Shah set out in the 18th century to unify Nepal. Its fortified palace, Gorkha Durbar, crowns a ridge about 300 m above the bazaar, with a Kalika temple, Gorakhnath cave and Himalayan views. Allow half a day.
intro: Gorkha lies 24 km north of the Prithvi Highway at Abu Khaireni, in the hills between the Marsyangdi and Daraudi rivers. The Shah family established a kingdom here in 1559, and for two centuries Gorkha was one of dozens of small hill states. In 1723 Prithvi Narayan Shah was born in the palace on the ridge. Becoming king in 1743, he spent the next 25 years conquering the Kathmandu Valley and the surrounding principalities, laying the foundations of the modern state of Nepal. The word Gurkha, used for Nepal's famous soldiers, comes from this town.

The main sight is Gorkha Durbar, a fortress-palace and temple complex built along the crest of the ridge with carved wooden windows, brick walls and stone courtyards. It contains the Kalika temple, sacred to the Shah kings, the room where Prithvi Narayan Shah is said to have been born, and below it the Gorakhnath cave shrine. On clear days from October to March the view to the north takes in Manaslu, Himalchuli, Baudha Himal and the Ganesh Himal.

Gorkha district was the epicentre area of the April 2015 earthquake, and the palace was badly damaged; it has since been restored, though some work may still be in progress. In the bazaar below, the Gorkha Museum in the old lower palace tells the story of the dynasty. Gorkha is a natural stop on a pilgrimage or heritage route between Kathmandu and Pokhara, usually combined with Manakamana. One night lets you climb to the palace in the cool morning light.
facts: Gorkha Durbar, Kalika temple, birthplace of Prithvi Narayan Shah

highlights.title: Gorkha Durbar
highlights.text: The fortress-palace runs along the ridge top with brick walls, carved peacock windows and wooden struts. Walk through its courtyards to see where the Shah kings held court and planned their campaigns, and look out from the terraces over the Gorkha valley and the Himalaya.

highlights.title: Kalika temple
highlights.text: The temple of the goddess Kalika inside the Durbar is one of the most revered Shakti shrines in Nepal and was the royal family's own temple. Only designated priests enter the inner sanctum; pilgrims worship at the courtyard. Sacrifices are made during Dashain and on auspicious days.

highlights.title: Gorakhnath cave
highlights.text: Below the southern side of the palace, a rock cave shrine honours Guru Gorakhnath, the yogi saint from whom the town and the Gurkhas take their name. Yogis of the Kanphata order serve here. It is a quiet, atmospheric stop on the way up or down.

highlights.title: The climb from the bazaar
highlights.text: A stone stairway of roughly 1,500 steps climbs about 300 m from the bazaar to the palace, taking 45 minutes to an hour. A road now reaches part of the way, leaving a 10–15 minute walk for those who cannot manage the full climb.

highlights.title: Gorkha Museum
highlights.text: The Tallo Durbar, a 19th century palace in a garden in the bazaar, now houses a museum of the Shah dynasty, weapons, coins, manuscripts and royal portraits. It gives context before you climb to the hilltop palace.

highlights.title: Upallo Kot viewpoint
highlights.text: Above the Durbar, a further climb of about 20–30 minutes along the ridge leads to the old fort site of Upallo Kot. The view here is wider and quieter, with the Manaslu range filling the northern horizon on clear mornings.

how_to_reach.text: From Kathmandu, drive west on the Prithvi Highway to Abu Khaireni, about 8 km past Mugling, then north for 24 km on a paved road to Gorkha Bazaar: about 140 km in 5–5.5 hours. From Pokhara it is about 110 km via Damauli and Dumre to Abu Khaireni, 3–3.5 hours. Manakamana's cable car base at Kurintar is about 45 km away, 1.5 hours. Local buses run from Kathmandu and Pokhara.

From Gorkha Bazaar, the stone staircase to Gorkha Durbar takes 45–60 minutes uphill. Vehicles can drive part of the way up the ridge on a newer road, leaving a short walk. Allow 30–40 minutes for the descent on the steps.

where_to_stay: Gorkha has simple 2- to 3-star hotels in and around the bazaar and a few small resorts on the hillsides outside town, with standards a step below Pokhara or Bandipur. They are clean and adequate for one night, serve Nepali and Indian food, and some have rooms with a view of the Durbar or the Himalaya. Pilgrims usually stay one night to climb to the palace in the morning light. Travellers who prefer more comfort can visit Gorkha as a half-day stop and continue to Bandipur (The Old Inn, about 1.5–2 hours) or Pokhara the same evening.
tips: Climb to Gorkha Durbar early in the morning for cooler air, clearer mountain views and fewer school groups.
Leather belts, bags and shoes are not allowed in the Kalika temple area; leave them with your driver.
Photography is restricted inside the temple, so ask before using a camera near shrines.
Carry water for the climb, as there are only a few small stalls on the stairway.
Visit the Gorkha Museum in the bazaar before climbing, so the palace makes more sense.

experiences.title: Climb to Gorkha Durbar and the ridge top
experiences.summary: Climb about 1,500 stone steps from Gorkha Bazaar to the hilltop palace of the Shah kings, explore its courtyards and carved windows, and look north to Manaslu. A guide explains how a small hill kingdom unified Nepal in the 18th century.
body: Start at the foot of the stairway near the bazaar early in the morning. The steps climb about 300 m through scrub forest and past small shrines, with resting points and views back over the town. Fit walkers reach the top in 45 minutes; most people take about an hour. If the climb is too much, your driver can take you up the newer road part of the way, leaving 10–15 minutes on foot.

Gorkha Durbar stretches along the ridge as a series of brick and timber buildings around courtyards. Look for the carved peacock and lattice windows, the wooden roof struts with deities and the thick defensive walls. Your guide shows you the area associated with the birth of Prithvi Narayan Shah in 1723, the royal quarters and the platforms from which, according to tradition, the young king looked east towards the Kathmandu Valley he would later conquer.

Parts of the complex were badly damaged in the 2015 earthquake and have been restored using traditional materials; some sections may be under repair. From the terraces, the view north on clear mornings takes in Manaslu, Himalchuli and Baudha Himal. Walk another 20–30 minutes up to Upallo Kot for a wider panorama, then descend by the steps, passing the Gorakhnath cave. Allow about three hours for the climb, the palace and the descent, and carry water, as stalls on the stairway are few.

faqs.q: How many steps are there to Gorkha Durbar?
faqs.a: Roughly 1,500 stone steps lead from Gorkha Bazaar to the palace, gaining about 300 m. The climb takes 45–60 minutes at an easy pace with rests. A road now reaches part of the way up the ridge, so visitors who cannot manage the full stairway can drive up and walk the last 10–15 minutes.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Gorkha Durbar?
faqs.a: A modest entry fee is charged for foreign visitors, roughly NPR 200–500, with lower rates for SAARC and Nepali visitors. Fees are set by the local authority and can change, so check current status before you travel. The Gorkha Museum in the bazaar charges a separate ticket.

faqs.q: Was Gorkha Durbar damaged in the 2015 earthquake?
faqs.a: Yes. Gorkha district was the epicentre area of the April 2015 earthquake, and the palace suffered serious damage. It has since been restored using traditional brick and timber, and the complex is open to visitors. Some sections may still be closed for work, so expect occasional scaffolding.

experiences.title: Gorkha Kalika and Gorakhnath cave darshan
experiences.summary: Worship at the Kalika temple inside Gorkha Durbar, the royal shrine of the Shah kings and one of Nepal's most powerful goddess temples, then visit the Gorakhnath cave below the palace. A key stop on any Manakamana–Gorkha pilgrimage.
body: The Kalika temple stands within the palace complex on the ridge. For centuries it was the private shrine of the Shah kings, and the goddess Kalika is believed to have guided the conquests of Prithvi Narayan Shah. The image is kept in an inner sanctum that only designated priests may enter, so pilgrims make their offerings in the courtyard: flowers, red powder, incense, coconut and sweets. Priests return prasad and tika.

Worship is busiest on Tuesdays and Saturdays and during Dashain, especially on the eighth and ninth days, when large numbers of animals are sacrificed and the palace fills with devotees. Pilgrims who prefer not to witness sacrifice should visit on other days and in the early morning. Leather is not allowed, and photography of the shrine is generally not permitted. Ask your guide which days are quietest during the week of your visit.

A short walk down the southern side of the ridge brings you to the Gorakhnath cave, a rock shelter shrine to Guru Gorakhnath, the Nath yogi revered by the Shah kings, attended by yogis with large earrings of the Kanphata order. It is quiet and cool, and devotees offer lamps and incense. Many pilgrims time this darshan after Manakamana, making it a two-goddess circuit in one or two days. Allow an hour for both shrines.

faqs.q: Can pilgrims see the Kalika idol in Gorkha?
faqs.a: No. The image of Kalika in Gorkha Durbar is kept in an inner sanctum that only designated priests enter, a long-standing tradition of the royal shrine. Pilgrims offer worship in the temple courtyard, and priests carry offerings inside and return prasad. This is normal practice and the darshan is still considered complete.

faqs.q: When is the best time for Gorkha Kalika darshan?
faqs.a: Weekday mornings outside festivals are calm and give time for prayers. Tuesdays and Saturdays are busier, and Dashain, which falls in September or October, draws very large crowds and many animal sacrifices. Festival dates follow the lunar calendar and change each year, so check current dates before you travel.

faqs.q: Who was Gorakhnath and why is Gorkha named after him?
faqs.a: Gorakhnath was a medieval yogi and founder of the Nath tradition, widely revered in Nepal and North India. Legend holds that he blessed the young Shah ruler, and the town of Gorkha, and later the word Gurkha, are traced to his name. The cave below Gorkha Durbar is his main shrine here.

experiences.title: Gorkha Museum in the Tallo Durbar
experiences.summary: The lower palace in Gorkha Bazaar now houses a museum on the Shah dynasty and the unification of Nepal: weapons, coins, royal clothing, manuscripts and portraits, in a square palace set in a garden. A good shaded stop before or after the hilltop climb.
body: The Tallo Durbar, or lower palace, stands in a walled garden in the centre of Gorkha Bazaar. It is a square, two-storey Newar-style building around a courtyard, with carved windows and wooden pillars, built in the 19th century as a residence for members of the royal family. Today it is managed as the Gorkha Museum and is one of the better regional museums in Nepal. Its garden makes a pleasant, shaded break after the drive.

Exhibits cover the founding of the Gorkha kingdom in 1559, the life and campaigns of Prithvi Narayan Shah, and the later Shah kings. You will see swords, khukuris and firearms, coins, seals and royal documents, costumes, ornaments and portraits. Panels in Nepali and English explain how the unification campaigns moved east across the hills to Nuwakot and the Kathmandu Valley between the 1740s and 1769. Labels are concise, so a guide adds a great deal.

Allow an hour. The museum is a short walk from most hotels and the bus park, so it fits the afternoon you arrive in Gorkha, with the climb to the hilltop palace saved for the following morning. Like most government museums in Nepal it has a weekly closing day and shorter winter hours, so check current timings before you travel. Photography rules inside the galleries vary, so ask at the ticket counter before taking pictures of the exhibits.

faqs.q: Is the Gorkha Museum worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are interested in Nepal's history. It explains the rise of the Shah dynasty and the unification of Nepal, which makes the hilltop palace far more meaningful. It is small, shaded and flat, so it suits seniors and families. Allow about an hour.

faqs.q: What are the Gorkha Museum timings?
faqs.a: Government museums in Nepal usually open around 10 am and close between 3 and 5 pm depending on season, with one weekly closing day and closures on some public holidays. Timings change, so check current status before you travel or ask your hotel in Gorkha.

faqs.q: How far is the Gorkha Museum from Gorkha Durbar?
faqs.a: The museum is in the bazaar at the foot of the ridge, while Gorkha Durbar is about 300 m higher on the hilltop. The stairway between them takes 45–60 minutes up. Most visitors see the museum on arrival and climb to the palace the next morning.

faqs.q: Why is Gorkha important in Nepal's history?
faqs.a: Gorkha was the seat of the Shah kings. Prithvi Narayan Shah was born here in 1723 and, from 1743, led campaigns that conquered the Kathmandu Valley in 1768–69 and joined dozens of hill states into one kingdom, the basis of modern Nepal. The Gurkha soldiers take their name from the town.

faqs.q: How far is Gorkha from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: About 140 km, a drive of 5–5.5 hours along the Prithvi Highway to Abu Khaireni and then 24 km north to Gorkha Bazaar. Traffic and road works between Naubise and Mugling can add time. Combining Manakamana on the way makes a full day.

faqs.q: How far is Gorkha from Pokhara?
faqs.a: About 110 km, around 3–3.5 hours by car via Damauli, Dumre and Abu Khaireni. The last 24 km from the highway are on a winding hill road. Gorkha works well as a day trip from Pokhara for a fit traveller, but an overnight stay is more relaxed.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see Gorkha Durbar?
faqs.a: Allow 3 hours: about an hour for the climb up the stone steps, an hour exploring the palace, Kalika temple courtyard and views, and 30–45 minutes for the descent via the Gorakhnath cave. Add an hour for the Gorkha Museum in the bazaar.

faqs.q: Is Gorkha worth visiting for foreign tourists?
faqs.a: Yes, for travellers interested in history, architecture and pilgrimage. It is far less visited than Bandipur or Pokhara, so you will meet more Nepali pilgrims than tourists. Combine it with Manakamana or Bandipur rather than making a long special trip only for Gorkha.

faqs.q: Can seniors climb to Gorkha Durbar?
faqs.a: The full stairway of about 1,500 steps is demanding for seniors. A road now goes part of the way up the ridge, leaving a 10–15 minute walk with some steps, which most seniors manage slowly. Go in the cool morning and carry water.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Gorkha?
faqs.a: October to March has dry weather and clear views of Manaslu and Himalchuli from the palace. Dashain, in September or October, brings large crowds and sacrifices to the Kalika temple. April and May are warm and hazy, and June to September is wet.

faqs.q: Is there good accommodation in Gorkha?
faqs.a: Gorkha has simple 2- to 3-star hotels in the bazaar and a few small resorts outside town. They are clean and fine for one night but not luxurious. Travellers wanting heritage character often stay in Bandipur instead, about 1.5–2 hours away.

Gorkha district is the gateway to the Manaslu region and to Gurung villages such as Barpak and Laprak, reached by road from Gorkha. These are separate multi-day trips. From the bazaar itself, the walk to Gorkha Durbar and Upallo Kot makes a good half-day hike.
